sources.title: Benchmarking and Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
sources.finding: Boundary identification and utility must be tested separately. BIPIA studies both prompting and training defenses; its simulated, non-multiturn cases cannot establish complete protection.
sources.decision: Implement independent inspectors; defer model training.
sources.review_scope: Selected substantive full-text method/design, evaluation and scope/discussion sections; not every appendix. Limits without explicit author statements are engineering scope assessments.

sources.title: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
sources.finding: StruQ separates instruction and data through formatting plus training. Its own limitations include residual adaptive attacks and a narrower programmatic-application scope. A gateway delimiter alone would not implement StruQ.
sources.decision: Preserve explicit trust boundaries; do not rewrite prompts as an authorization defense.
sources.review_scope: Selected substantive full-text method/design, evaluation and scope/discussion sections; not every appendix. Limits without explicit author statements are engineering scope assessments.

sources.title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
sources.finding: The instruction hierarchy is trained through synthetic composition/ignorance examples and evaluated for robustness and over-refusal. The paper acknowledges remaining adversarial and multimodal work.
sources.decision: Keep authorization independent of model obedience; retain benign-use tests.
sources.review_scope: Selected substantive full-text method/design, evaluation and scope/discussion sections; not every appendix. Limits without explicit author statements are engineering scope assessments.

sources.title: Aligning LLMs to Be Robust Against Prompt Injection (SecAlign, v1)
sources.finding: SecAlign uses preference optimization toward desirable and away from injected responses. The v1 title is Aligning LLMs to Be Robust Against Prompt Injection. It requires clear input separation and does not claim complete security.
sources.decision: Defer training; expose a veto-only adapter boundary for deployment-owned defenses.
sources.review_scope: Selected substantive full-text method/design, evaluation and scope/discussion sections; not every appendix. Limits without explicit author statements are engineering scope assessments.

sources.title: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
sources.finding: Spotlighting marks untrusted content through delimiters, datamarking or encoding. Its keyword attack evaluation and older models limit generalization; encoding can damage utility.
sources.decision: Reject automatic result re-encoding; provide explicit result-inspection integration.
sources.review_scope: Selected substantive full-text method/design, evaluation and scope/discussion sections; not every appendix. Limits without explicit author statements are engineering scope assessments.

sources.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
sources.finding: AgentHarm measures harmful multi-step compliance with synthetic tools, rather than general safety. English prompts and constrained initial user attacks limit coverage.
sources.decision: Retain concrete effect checks and separate success from denial outcomes.

sources.title: Agent-SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
sources.finding: Agent-SafetyBench covers varied risk categories and uses a calibrated learned scorer. Its own scorer construction shows that a generic model judge is imperfect.
sources.decision: No classifier verdict grants access; exceptions/timeouts deny.
sources.review_scope: Selected substantive full-text method/design, evaluation and scope/discussion sections; not every appendix. Limits without explicit author statements are engineering scope assessments.

sources.title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents
sources.finding: ASB formalizes prompt, observation, memory and backdoor attack surfaces, with several defense families. Versions differ in benchmark counts; results depend on chosen agents/tools.
sources.decision: Add a result boundary and immutable per-call contexts; do not invent workflow provenance.

sources.title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
sources.finding: AgentPoison attacks retrieval memories through optimized triggers and reports retrieval/action/environment outcomes separately. Its attacker has embedder access, with transfer studied empirically.
sources.decision: Keep shared model memory out of the gateway; test actual upstream effects.

sources.title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks
sources.finding: Adaptive jailbreaks show that a fixed prompt defense needs evaluation against an attacker that responds to it. Access assumptions and model versions matter.
sources.decision: Use deterministic authorization as the floor; retain pluggable inspectors without immunity claims.

sources.title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
sources.finding: ToolLLM builds tool-use trajectories and retrieval over a large API inventory. External API availability and automatic grading affect reproducibility.
sources.decision: Bound discovery and avoid mistaking generated trajectories for real integration evidence.

sources.title: API-Bank: A Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
